You shift emphasis from the beginning to another part of the sentence by using what, that and who phrases as subjects.

Usually, we focus on the person doing the action in this case.
Example: It makes a lot of sense.

If we wish to place emphasis on another part of the sentence, we isolate that part and package up the rest of the information into a what-phrase (or sometimes a that clause.)
Example: What you said makes a lot of sense.

What or Who serves as a placeholder for the content of the noun phrase that has been moved to the end of the sentence. The effect is that more emphasis is placed on the initial content.
Example: What we are currently working on is a complete digital transformation so as to adapt to the way people access information.

A “what-phrase” is made up of: what + pronoun + verb phrase
Example: What we normally do is sort the stack of applications we receive at the fair into three piles.
“What-phrases” are often used to:<ul><li>to introduce a new topic; <li>to give a reason, instruction, or explanation; <li>or to correct something that has been said or done.
What headhunters do is basically weed out people who don't have the qualifications.

What I am really interested in is getting my foot in the door.
In English, all sentences are in either “active” or “passive” voice.

The active voice focus on the thing which is doing the action (i.e. the subject of the sentence) and the thing receiving the action (i.e. the object). Most sentences in English are in the active voice.
<ul><li><span class="italic">If you want the job, I suggest applying for it.
We use the passive when the ‘doer' (agent) of the action it not so important. We are not interested in knowing who did the action. Our attention is on the object.
<ul><li><span class="italic">Applying for the job is suggested if you want the position.
Here's some more information about the passive of modal verbs.

1. The Passive is formed by [thing receiving the action] + be + past participle + (by) + (thing doing the action)
  2. The passive can be used when the “doer” is unknown, irrelevant, or you want to be vague about who is responsible for the action.
  3. You can also use the passive to talk about a general truth.

Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self Assessment.

images.text:
Adam: So, this is a publishing company?
Headhunter: Yes and no. What we are currently working on is a complete digital transformation so as to adapt to the way people access information.
Adam: That sounds bang up to date. Are you currently hiring?
Headhunter: As a matter of fact, we are. A flair for the English language along with flawless grammar is needed for this job.
Adam: Are there any other requirements for the position?
Headhunter: A degree in Journalism or Creative Writing is required. A minimum 1 year writing experience is recommended. Ability to multitask and meet tight deadlines is needed. And strong verbal and written communication skills are demanded.

Adam: OK. I seem to have the right educational background and level of experience. How do you go about hiring?
Headhunter: What we normally do is to sort of stack the applications we receive at the fair into three piles: potential candidates, those who are worth a second look, and the “nos”.
Adam: So, what headhunters do is basically weed out people who don't have the qualifications, right?
Headhunter: Yes. What we have discovered is that most applications are pathetic. Very few people here are “employee material”.
Adam: What you said makes a lot of sense. I'm still working on becoming employable.

Headhunter: Also, this is an entry position. Most experienced candidates are not willing to work for peanuts.
Adam: At this point, what I am really interested in is getting my foot in the door. Do you think I stand a chance?
Headhunter: You stand as good a chance as anyone. I must warn you: applying for the job is suggested if you want the position.
Adam: Great. Can I leave my resume with you?
Headhunter: Do you have a cover letter as well?
Adam: Well … I don't have one handy but I'll be right back!
